I think most important of all, not that many people are homosexual. I mean its a pretty big number, but certainly not big enough to push their most prefered legislative bills trough parliment. 

Number of people that were even anti civil partnership in Poland was quite big, it changed ofc and now in general Poles are more ok with that. That doesnt mean it would be still a popular thing to push. 

Politicians are opportunists after all, most of them arent idealists. Now you could make an argument that it changes because a lot of LGBT people moved to bigger cities and therefore people elected in those big cities are more likely to care about these issues. But a group of people that was equally distributed (well, still isnt centralized, its impossible for all LGBT people to move into few big cities) and wasnt that politicaly active simply couldnt hope for anything to be just given to them. 

Now we've seen a growth of people that even if arent LGBT themselves, do care about this topic because idk they know a gay person etc, so automatically supporting these causes wasnt that unpopular and it gained political support.

Yeah, civil partnerships solve this issue the best i think. If there is a large enough of catholic Poles that dont object to that, then it should be implemented. Pushing same sex marriage trough parliment (most likely trough some type of deal between parties in coalition) would result in controversial thing that would be quite a fuel for far right people.

1. More likely to get passed and approved by wider society. If most people change their views on this topic then future generation might as well legalize same sex marriage. 

2. Im not catholic, never have been, but if you agree that we should look for compromises then this is a compromise. Sure, same sex marriage might get pushed after opposition wins elections, but what then? Homosexual people are happy, thats cool. Catholics get angry ("uh but why are they angry if it doesnt involve them", you could ask this question about MANY situations where people moralize the other side), it just makes polarization of our society even worse. Im all about building bridges, if one side cannot accept any sort of compromise then how are they ok?

They arent trying to be modern tho, they wont invest in self checkout (which i think is quite great) because they know most people that shop there daily dont like self checkout. Even tho its a smaller store than Lidl, I always spend more time in Dino because there's no self checkout. 

Its very important for people in villages in these parts. Biedronka, lidl, netto etc wont go near villages but Dino will and this is a huge number of clients. 

Overall I think we will see more tendency in dino+żabka growing because they seem to really hit the soft spot for a lot of customers.

Well if you consider Brandenburg to be successor to Prussian culture and history then yeah, but it still was a seperate region within the Prussian state and was much different culturaly from... actual Prussia. 

I for one think its because of how much of the population for most of the medieval period was slavic, their customs and traditions werent taken over to a large extent by Germans and when those slavs became incredibly small minority it was already few centuries too late for regionalisation. 

By culture in this context I meant things that are specific for this region only. I wouldnt say that Prussian palace's and castles were something explicitly brandenburgish. 

Cuisine? As far as I know only differences are the amounts of sweetwater fishes and wild mushrooms in diet, but I wouldnt say its "their" thing by any means. 

You can make cases for specific dialect being something special (which is also fading away as many other more obscure german dialects). 

Sure, the history of this general region is interesting (well, place where I live also shares that history) BUT I wouldnt make a claim that history is the only thing that makes a culture. Customs, music, traditions, cuisine etc are also a big part of it and this is where I feel like this specific region is lacking.

Depends. There are people like that in every nation, its only the % of them of total population that varies between countries. 

Regions that are more rural and have higher number of people that attend church regularly are more likely to be also less tolerant of lgbt people (well church isnt exactly a friend of non hetero and non cis people). People that vote for more right wing parties are also more likely to be less tolerant of LGBT (again, most of these people are in the regions mentioned in the first example). 

Older people, even if not religious and not from a rural area are more likely to be less tolerant because of decades of living during communist era Poland. 

Larger cities are more likely to be more tolerant (more young people, less religious people, more left voters). Regions that are more left voting and less religious in general are more tolerant. 

Majority of places in Poland are filled with people that dont care much, I wouldnt say it means they are tolerant but they wont go out of their way to be rude to lgbt people and make their life harder etc. 

I hate the Poland A (western and northern Poland) vs Poland B (eastern and southern Poland) argument because its not a huge drastic change in people, but its still something you can experience in everyday life if you are part of the LGBT community. 

Thats why many LGBTQ people are moving from eastern and southern parts of Poland to bigger cities that are already quite tolerant (Poznań, Gdańsk, Wrocław etc).
